processing: The usual yellow tea path of kill-green, rolling, sealed yellowing (men huang) and drying; handling varies between bud-only needle tea and leafier strands.
harvest_season: Spring; the needle form uses spring buds with a short stem.
appearance_dry: Varies by style, from golden upright buds to curled, tippy strands.
appearance_liquor: Clear yellow, the 'yellow liquor' expected of the class.
appearance_wet: Yellow leaf or buds; needle-style buds stand upright when steeped in a glass.
taste_profile: Described as mellow and clean with a gentle sweetness; the exact cup depends on whether it is bud or leaf tea.

brewing.notes: General guidance for yellow tea. Use a glass for needle styles so you can watch the buds stand.

vintage_note: Usually sold as the current year's spring tea, and graded where standards apply; needle-style tea comes in top and first grades. As with other yellow teas, it is for drinking fresh rather than ageing.
description:
Yueyang Huang Cha is less one tea than the name for yellow tea from Yueyang in Hunan, on Dongting Lake. Under that heading sit the area's best-known teas: Junshan Yinzhen from Junshan island and Beigang Maojian from around Beigang near Kangwang.

The common thread is the class method: a green-tea-like start followed by sealed yellowing, in which warmth and moisture turn the leaf yellow and soften it. How long and how hard that goes differs by tea, so the leaf style matters more than the label.

Expect a mellow, sweet cup with little bitterness and clear yellow liquor. Brew below boiling, and use a glass for needle styles.

When buying, ask which tea you are getting. A generic 'Yueyang yellow tea' may be anything from upright buds to everyday strands, and the price should reflect that. Trying Junshan Yinzhen and Beigang Maojian side by side is the easiest way to see the range.
history: Hunan's yellow tea is long associated with the Dongting Lake area, but little is documented about Yueyang Huang Cha as a single named tea or when the umbrella name came into use. A firmer recent marker is that Junshan Yinzhen's making technique was placed on China's national intangible heritage list in its fifth batch in 2021, with Junshan district of Yueyang as the applicant.
